analogy.p: Imagine a very long loaf of bread (a long hydrocarbon chain) that nobody wants because it is too big to eat; the bakery (refinery) cuts it into shorter rolls that sell quickly. The knife is the heat and catalyst: it breaks the chain at certain points. Because you cannot make two perfect rolls from the same dough, one piece ends up as a thin breadstick (the alkene) that is useful for something else. This breaks down because real cracking happens at random places along the chain and the alkene has a different type of bond (a C=C double bond), not just a different size.

bullets: Cracking turns **surplus long-chain alkanes** into shorter alkanes and **alkenes**.
It is a **chemical change** (new substances form), unlike fractional distillation, which is a physical separation.
The specification wording: hydrocarbons can be **broken down (cracked)** to produce **smaller, more useful molecules**.
Cracking is a type of **thermal decomposition**: one substance breaks into two or more simpler ones when heated.
It is done on an industrial scale at oil refineries, directly after fractional distillation.
Short-chain products are used as **fuels** and the alkenes are used to make **polymers** and other chemicals.
Link: this is why the oil industry can supply the right mix of fuels even though crude oil contains the wrong mix.
core.h: What cracking is and why it is needed
core.p: **Cracking** is the process of breaking down **long-chain hydrocarbons** into **shorter, more useful molecules**. Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into fractions, but the fractions do not come out in the proportions that customers want. Large molecules such as those in fuel oil and bitumen are produced in greater amounts than the market needs, while small molecules such as those in petrol and kerosene are in higher demand. Cracking fixes this mismatch by turning some of the surplus large molecules into small ones. It also makes **alkenes**, which are the starting materials for plastics and many other chemicals.

bullets: **Small molecules** (short chains) are in **high demand** because they make good fuels.
**Large molecules** (long chains) are in **lower demand** and are often produced in surplus.
Small molecules are **more flammable**, have **lower boiling points** and are **less viscous**, so they burn easily and are easy to handle.
Large molecules are **viscous**, have **high boiling points** and are **hard to ignite**, so they are poor fuels.
Cracking converts a low-value surplus into high-value fuels and alkenes.
Examples of products used as fuels: petrol, kerosene, diesel, and gases such as LPG.
The mix of fractions in crude oil depends on the oil field, so refineries adjust how much they crack.
core.p: Different fractions of crude oil are needed in very different amounts. There is a **high demand for fuels with small molecules**, such as petrol (for cars), kerosene (for jet engines) and diesel. Fractions with long chains, such as fuel oil and bitumen, are in lower demand and the refinery would otherwise be left with a surplus it cannot sell. Because oil is expensive to extract and refine, it makes economic sense to convert the unwanted large molecules into products that sell at a higher price. This is a classic exam idea: cracking balances **supply with demand**.

bullets: Boiling point **increases** with chain length because longer molecules have stronger intermolecular forces.
Viscosity **increases** with chain length: long chains tangle and flow poorly (like treacle).
Flammability **decreases** with chain length: short chains vaporise and mix with oxygen more easily.
Ease of ignition: gases and petrol ignite easily; bitumen and fuel oil need heating first.
Cleaner burning: short chains burn more completely, with less soot.
Link to fractional distillation: the fractions near the top of the column are the short, volatile ones.
Link to combustion: complete combustion of any hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water.
core.h: Why small hydrocarbons make better fuels
core.p: A fuel needs to **vaporise and ignite easily** and burn cleanly. As the chain length increases, the **intermolecular forces** between molecules increase, so the boiling point rises and the liquid becomes more viscous. Short-chain molecules are held together by weak forces, so they evaporate readily and mix with air, which makes combustion easy. Long-chain molecules need much more energy to separate and tend to burn with a smoky flame, leaving soot. This is the reason there is a premium on the short fractions.

bullets: Reactant: a **long-chain alkane** (for example decane C10H22, or the heavier fractions such as diesel and fuel oil).
Products: a **shorter alkane** and one or more **alkenes**.
Cracking breaks **carbon-carbon single bonds**, so it is a **thermal decomposition** reaction.
It takes in energy to break bonds, so a high temperature is required.
The total number of carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms is the same before and after the reaction.
The alkene has **fewer hydrogen atoms** than the alkane with the same number of carbons, so it is **unsaturated**.
The products can be different on different occasions: a mixture is often formed.
core.h: The idea of breaking a large molecule into smaller ones
core.p: In cracking, **covalent C-C bonds** in a long alkane molecule are broken, so the large molecule splits into two or more smaller molecules. Breaking bonds needs energy, so cracking is **endothermic** overall and needs a high temperature. Atoms are conserved, so every carbon and hydrogen atom in the large molecule must appear in the products. A key point is that the products always include **at least one alkene**, a molecule with a C=C double bond, because there are not enough hydrogen atoms to make all the products alkanes.

bullets: Alkane general formula: **CnH2n+2** (for example C8H18, n = 8: 2n+2 = 18).
Alkene general formula: **CnH2n** (for example C2H4, n = 2: 2n = 4).
Splitting one alkane into **two alkanes** would need more hydrogen than is available, so it cannot happen on its own.
Hence products = **one alkane + one (or more) alkene(s)**.
Example check: C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4: carbons 8 + 2 = 10; hydrogens 18 + 4 = 22.
Counting rule: add up all the C and all the H on each side separately and compare.
Higher-tier style link: you may be asked to **balance** a cracking equation or **find the missing product** from the formulae.
core.h: Why alkenes must be formed (the hydrogen argument)
core.p: An alkane with n carbon atoms has the formula **CnH2n+2**, while an alkene has the formula **CnH2n**. If a long alkane splits into two smaller molecules, the total hydrogen is fixed. For example decane C10H22 splitting into two pieces with 8 and 2 carbons: an alkane with 8 carbons needs 18 hydrogens, leaving only 4 hydrogens for the 2-carbon piece, and a 2-carbon alkane would need 6. With only 4 hydrogens it becomes ethene, C2H4, which has a C=C double bond. This reasoning explains why cracking always makes alkenes and is a strong way to check an equation.

bullets: Step 1: the hydrocarbon is **heated until it vaporises**.
Step 2: the vapour is passed over a **hot catalyst** (for example zeolite or aluminium oxide).
The catalyst provides an **alternative pathway with lower activation energy**, so the reaction is faster at a lower temperature.
A catalyst is **not used up**, so it can be reused (although carbon deposits on it, so it is regenerated).
Catalytic cracking mainly produces **motor fuels** (petrol) and alkenes.
Exam phrase: "heated to a high temperature and passed over a hot catalyst".
Link to rates: a catalyst increases the rate without changing the products' overall energy change.
core.p: In **catalytic cracking** the long-chain hydrocarbons are first **heated to vaporise** them, and the vapour is then passed over a **hot catalyst**. The catalyst is a solid such as a **zeolite** (a form of aluminium silicate) or aluminium oxide. The catalyst provides a surface on which the molecules break apart, so the reaction is faster and works at a lower temperature than would otherwise be needed, saving energy. In industry this is done at a temperature of roughly 500 degrees C or above, but you do not need to learn the exact figure. The products are mostly shorter alkanes and alkenes that are used for fuels.

bullets: Hydrocarbon vapour is **mixed with steam** and heated to a very high temperature.
The mixture is **cooled rapidly** so that the products do not react further.
It gives a high yield of **ethene and propene**, which are used to make polymers.
Compared with catalytic cracking, it does not use a solid catalyst but it needs more energy.
Both methods are listed by the specification: you must know **catalytic cracking and steam cracking**.
Exam tip: if you are asked for the conditions, give both parts: **high temperature** and **catalyst** (or **steam**).
Link: the alkenes made are the monomers for addition polymerisation (for example ethene gives poly(ethene)).
core.p: In **steam cracking** the long-chain hydrocarbons are **mixed with steam** and heated to a **very high temperature** (typically above 800 degrees C) for a very short time. The steam dilutes the hydrocarbon so that the molecules are less likely to collide and recombine, and the high temperature supplies the energy to break the C-C bonds. The mixture is then cooled quickly to stop further reactions. Steam cracking gives a high proportion of **small alkenes** such as ethene and propene, so it is the main source of the raw materials for the plastics industry.

bullets: Apparatus: boiling tube, mineral wool soaked in liquid paraffin, catalyst chips, delivery tube, trough of water, gas collection tubes.
The catalyst is heated **strongly**; the mineral wool is heated **gently** so that the paraffin vaporises.
Gases are collected **over water** because alkenes and short alkanes are **insoluble (or only slightly soluble)** in water.
Test the gas with **bromine water**: if an alkene is present it goes from **orange to colourless**.
Safety: remove the **delivery tube from the water before stopping heating** to avoid **suck-back** (cold water sucked into hot glass, which can crack it).
Safety: wear safety glasses; hydrocarbons are **flammable**, so keep flames away from the collection area.
The first gas collected is mainly air pushed out of the apparatus, so the first tube is discarded.
core.p: A standard school demonstration cracks **liquid paraffin** (a mixture of long-chain alkanes). Mineral wool is soaked in the liquid paraffin and placed at one end of a hard-glass boiling tube, with a small amount of **catalyst** such as aluminium oxide pieces or broken porcelain next to it. The catalyst is heated strongly, and the paraffin is warmed gently so that its vapour passes over the hot catalyst. The gas that is produced is collected over water, because the gases are not very soluble in water, and is tested with bromine water to show that an alkene is present.

bullets: Shorter **alkanes**: used as fuels (for example petrol and diesel).
**Alkenes**: used to produce polymers such as poly(ethene) and poly(propene).
Alkenes are also a starting material for **alcohols (ethanol)** and many other chemicals.
The specification states that alkenes are used to produce polymers and as **starting materials for the production of many other chemicals**.
Alkenes are **more reactive** than alkanes because of the C=C double bond, which makes them useful chemical building blocks.
Link: alkanes are largely unreactive except for combustion; alkenes undergo addition reactions.
The mixture of products can be separated by **distillation** because the molecules have different boiling points.
core.h: Products of cracking and their uses
core.p: The products of cracking include **alkanes and alkenes**. The shorter alkanes are used as **fuels**, for example petrol, kerosene and diesel, to meet the high demand for fuels with small molecules. The alkenes are much more reactive than alkanes and are used to make **polymers** (plastics) and as **starting materials** for many other chemicals, such as ethanol and antifreeze. Sometimes hydrogen is also formed. This is why cracking is valuable: it produces both fuels and feedstock for the chemical industry.

bullets: Reagent: **bromine water** (orange / yellow-brown).
Positive result (alkene): **orange to colourless**.
Negative result (alkane): remains **orange**.
The test works because alkenes are **unsaturated** and undergo **addition reactions** with bromine.
Write the word **colourless**, never "clear" or "goes see-through".
This is the standard test used to show that cracking has taken place.
Link: saturated = only single C-C bonds; unsaturated = at least one C=C double bond.
core.h: Testing the products: alkane or alkene?
core.p: To show that a cracking product is an alkene, add **bromine water** to it and shake. **Alkenes** decolourise bromine water, so the colour changes from **orange (brown) to colourless** because the bromine adds across the C=C double bond. **Alkanes** do not react, so the bromine water stays **orange**. Only the colour change to colourless counts as a positive result: a mark scheme will not accept "clear" because the solution is clear to start with, just coloured.

bullets: Finding a missing product: C14H30 -> C8H18 + ? gives C6H12 (subtract: C 14-8 = 6, H 30-18 = 12), which is an alkene (CnH2n with n = 6).
Check the product type: if the formula fits CnH2n, it is an alkene; if CnH2n+2, an alkane.
State symbols are not usually needed unless asked.
core.p: The specification requires you to **balance chemical equations** for cracking, given the formulae of the reactants and products. The method is to count atoms on each side. First balance the carbon atoms, then check the hydrogen atoms: if the carbons balance, the hydrogens should also balance when the correct alkane and alkene formulae are used. If a product is unknown, subtract the known products from the reactant to find it. Always check by recounting both elements at the end.

bullets: Cracking is **endothermic**: bonds are broken, so energy is taken in.
A **high temperature** gives molecules enough energy to break their bonds.
A **catalyst** lowers the activation energy, so a lower temperature or faster reaction is possible.
Too long at high temperature can cause **coking** (carbon deposits), which blocks the catalyst.
Steam: dilutes the hydrocarbon and reduces carbon formation.
Industrial cost: high temperatures use lots of energy, so refineries balance costs against the value of products.
Link to Paper 2 energy changes: bond breaking = endothermic; bond making = exothermic.
core.h: Energy and conditions: why heat is needed
core.p: Breaking strong covalent C-C bonds needs a lot of energy, so cracking needs a **high temperature**. This makes cracking an **endothermic** process overall: energy is taken in from the surroundings (the furnace). A catalyst does not change the energy needed to reach the products overall, but it lowers the **activation energy** by providing an alternative reaction route, so less heat is needed to get the reaction going. Steam cracking uses a very high temperature but a short time to avoid unwanted side-reactions such as formation of carbon (coke).

bullets: Fractional distillation: **physical**, separates by **boiling point**, no new substances.
Cracking: **chemical**, breaks bonds, **new substances** (including alkenes) are made.
Distillation uses **heat and a fractionating column** with a temperature gradient.
Cracking uses **heat plus a catalyst** or **steam**.
Distillation: input is crude oil. Cracking: input is **long-chain fractions** such as diesel, fuel oil.
Distillation products are all alkanes (mostly); cracking gives alkanes **and alkenes**.
Together they let refineries match product output to market demand.
core.p: These two processes are used together in a refinery but they are very different. **Fractional distillation** is a **physical** separation based on differences in boiling points, so the molecules are not changed. **Cracking** is a **chemical** reaction that changes the molecules themselves, producing new substances. A common exam error is to describe cracking as a way of separating crude oil; it is not. Cracking works on the fractions produced by distillation, usually the heavier ones.

bullets: Compare **supply** with **demand** for each fraction; identify the **surplus** and the **shortage**.
State that surplus **long-chain** molecules are cracked to make more **small, useful** molecules.
Use data: quote values from the table or chart to support your point.
Identify an alkene by its formula CnH2n or by a positive bromine water test.
Mention **both** products: shorter alkane (fuel) and alkene (polymer feedstock).
In a 6-mark answer include **conditions** (high temperature, catalyst or steam), a **balanced equation**, and **uses**.
Always give units and use the chemical formulae correctly: C2H4 not CH4.
core.p: Questions on cracking often give a **table or bar chart** of the percentage of each fraction in crude oil compared with the demand for each fraction. Look for fractions where the supply is larger than the demand (usually the long chains) and explain that these are cracked. You may also be asked to interpret formulae, for example to decide whether a product is an alkene from CnH2n. For a 6-mark question, structure your answer as: what cracking is, how it is done (conditions), what is made, and why it is useful.

exam: Command word **Describe/Explain cracking**: give what it is (breaking long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter ones), the conditions (high temperature, hot catalyst or steam) and the products (alkane + alkene).
**1 mark**: define cracking, or give one use of the alkene (making polymers).
**2 marks**: "Give two ways cracking is carried out" - catalytic cracking and steam cracking.
**2 marks**: describe the test for an alkene: add bromine water, shake; orange to colourless.
**3 marks**: balance a cracking equation and state why one product is an alkene (formula CnH2n / double bond).
**4 marks**: explain why cracking is done - high demand for small molecules, surplus of large ones, cracking gives more fuel and alkenes.
**6 marks**: plan the answer with sections: purpose, process and conditions, equation, products and uses, test; link each point to a reason (why, not just what).
Use **supply and demand** language: "surplus", "higher demand", "more useful".
Data questions: quote figures from the table or chart, and compare supply with demand for each fraction.
Do not confuse cracking with fractional distillation: physical separation vs chemical breakdown.
Check every equation by counting C and H on each side before moving on.

mistakes.r: Cracking is a chemical reaction that breaks long molecules into shorter ones; fractional distillation does the separating.
mistakes.w: Cracking separates crude oil into fractions.

mistakes.r: Cracking makes a shorter alkane and an alkene, because there is not enough hydrogen to make two alkanes.
Bromine water goes from orange to colourless; "clear" is not accepted.
mistakes.w: Bromine water goes clear with an alkene.

mistakes.r: There is lower demand for them than for small molecules, so cracking matches supply to demand.
mistakes.w: Large molecules are cracked because they are not useful at all.

mistakes.r: A catalyst is not used up; it speeds up the reaction by providing an alternative pathway.
mistakes.w: The catalyst gets used up in cracking.

mistakes.r: Cracking is endothermic because bonds are broken, and a high temperature is needed.
Check atoms: the carbons add to 11, not 10; use C2H4, which gives C 10 and H 22.
mistakes.w: Unbalanced equation such as C10H22 -> C8H18 + C3H6.

mistakes.r: Alkenes are unsaturated because they have a C=C double bond.
The conditions are a high temperature with a hot catalyst (catalytic cracking) or with steam (steam cracking).
mistakes.w: Cracking uses fractional distillation conditions only.

summary: The specification asks you to know that long-chain hydrocarbons can be cracked into smaller, more useful molecules by catalytic cracking and steam cracking, to balance cracking equations, and that the products include alkanes (fuels) and alkenes (used for polymers and other chemicals). It matters because it explains how a refinery matches its output to demand and links to alkenes, bromine water and polymers.

terms.d: The breaking down of long-chain hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful molecules, by heating with a catalyst or steam.
A reaction in which a substance is broken down into two or more simpler substances by heating.
Cracking in which hydrocarbon vapour is passed over a hot catalyst.
Cracking in which hydrocarbons are mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature.
A saturated hydrocarbon with only single carbon-carbon bonds and the general formula CnH2n+2.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing a carbon-carbon double bond, with the general formula CnH2n.
A compound made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
Containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.
A mixture of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points, separated from crude oil.
How easily a liquid flows; long-chain hydrocarbons are more viscous.
How easily a substance catches fire; short-chain hydrocarbons are more flammable.
A very large molecule made from many small repeating units (monomers) joined together.
An orange solution used to test for alkenes, which decolourise it.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings.

worked.q: Balance the equation for cracking dodecane: C12H26 -> C8H18 + ?C2H4. (2 marks)
steps: Carbon: 12 on the left; 8 are in C8H18, so 4 carbons remain in the C2H4 units.
4 carbons in C2H4 units means 4/2 = 2 molecules of C2H4.
Hydrogen check: 18 + (2 x 4) = 26, which equals the 26 on the left.

worked.q: 0.50 mol of decane, C10H22, is cracked completely to octane and ethene. Calculate the mass of ethene formed. Mr values: C = 12, H = 1. (3 marks)
steps: Equation: C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4, so 1 mol of decane gives 1 mol of ethene.
Mr of ethene C2H4 = (2 x 12) + (4 x 1) = 28.
Mass = moles x Mr = 0.50 x 28 = 14 g.
Check: decane 0.50 x 142 = 71 g; octane 0.50 x 114 = 57 g; 57 g + 14 g = 71 g, so mass is conserved.

worked.ans: Crude oil contains too many long-chain hydrocarbons and not enough short-chain ones, but there is a higher demand for short-chain fuels. Cracking breaks the long chains down into shorter alkanes for fuels and alkenes, which are used to make polymers and other chemicals.
worked.q: Explain why oil companies crack some of the fractions obtained from crude oil. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: crude oil contains more long-chain hydrocarbons than are needed (surplus / lower demand).
Mark 2: there is a higher demand for shorter-chain hydrocarbons for use as fuels (such as petrol).
Mark 3: cracking breaks long-chain molecules into shorter, more useful ones.
Mark 4: it also produces alkenes, which are used to make polymers and other chemicals.
